items.text: A Wayne County homeowner's insurer receives a written appraisal demand on June 1. By what date must the insurer notify the homeowner of its chosen appraiser's identity?
B. June 21 — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) requires each party to select an appraiser and notify the other within 20 days after receipt of the written demand; June 1 plus 20 days is June 21.
The two party appraisers in a Macomb County fire claim cannot agree on an umpire after 15 days. Who may ask a circuit judge to select one, and from which county?

B. Either party, from the county where the loss occurred or the property is located — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) allows either the insured or the insurer to ask a judge of the circuit court for the county where the loss occurred or where the property is located to select an umpire.
A restoration contractor's insured client gets a signed appraisal report from her own appraiser and the umpire, but the carrier's appraiser refuses to sign. Is the amount of loss binding?

A. Yes, a written agreement signed by any 2 of the 3 (two appraisers plus umpire) sets the amount of loss — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) states that written agreement signed by any 2 of the 3 (the two appraisers and the umpire) sets the amount of the loss; unanimity is not required.
Under MCL 500.2833(1)(m), the appraisers must set the amount of loss and actual cash value in what format?
B. As to each item, on a line-item basis — The statute requires the appraisers to 'set the amount of the loss and actual cash value as to each item,' meaning a line-item basis, not a lump sum.

An Auto-Owners policyholder's carrier admits the fire is a covered event but disputes only whether specific kitchen cabinets qualify as covered 'improvements and betterments.' Per Kwaiser and Cantina, who should decide this dispute?

B. The appraisers, because coverage for the fire is admitted and only amount/scope remains — Kwaiser and Cantina hold that once coverage for the event is admitted, disputes over whether specific damaged items fall within a covered category are amount-of-loss/scope disputes for the appraisers, not coverage questions for a court.

In Maksym v Auto-Owners Ins Co (2026), the trial court initially treated the carrier's August 18, 2022 letter as a single, complete denial of all outstanding claims for statute-of-limitations purposes. What did the Court of Appeals say about that approach?

C. It found a genuine question of fact about whether the letter's treatment of the second-floor and other kitchen claims was equivocal or even revoked, reversing in part — The Court of Appeals held the letter formally and explicitly denied the plumbing and ALE claims, but found a fact question on whether the bathroom/kitchen language amounted to a formal denial, reversing the trial court's blanket treatment in part.

A homeowner in Oakland County notifies her carrier of a fire loss on January 5. The carrier never formally denies liability but disputes the amount for eight months while requesting more documentation. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(q) as applied in Smitham and Maksym, is the insured's suit-limitation clock still running during those eight months?

C. No, the clock is tolled from notice of loss until the insurer formally denies liability, and no formal denial has occurred — MCL 500.2833(1)(q), rooted in Tom Thomas Organization v Reliance Ins Co (1976) and applied in Smitham (2012) and Maksym (2026), tolls the suit clock from notice until a formal denial; ongoing document requests without an explicit, unequivocal denial do not end tolling.
Which Michigan Supreme Court case rejected a lower court's refusal to enforce a one-year contractual suit-limitation period on the ground that the period was 'unreasonable'?

A. Rory v Continental Ins Co — Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005), held a court may not refuse to enforce an unambiguous contract provision merely because it deems it 'unreasonable'; only law/public-policy violations or traditional contract defenses apply.

A public adjuster is retained by an insured on a 10 percent contingency fee and is later named as the insured's party appraiser in a written MCL 500.2833(1)(m) demand. What must the demand letter do, per White v State Farm?

B. Disclose to the carrier that the contingency-fee agreement exists — White v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 293 Mich App 419 (2011), held a contingency fee does not disqualify a party appraiser from being 'independent,' but the opposing party must be made aware the contingency-fee agreement exists.

A signed appraisal award sets a total loss amount, but the insured later learns the umpire secretly accepted a payment from the carrier's appraiser during deliberations. What is the insured's best legal basis to challenge the award under Dupree v Auto-Owners Ins Co?

A. Fraud or bad faith in the appraisal process — Dupree confirms judicial review is limited to bad faith, fraud, misconduct, or manifest mistake; a secretly compromised umpire is a fraud/misconduct scenario, one of the narrow recognized grounds.

An appraisal award in a Genesee County fire claim states the actual cash value of destroyed personal property but does not address replacement cost. The insured has not yet replaced any items. Per Dupree, is the insured automatically entitled to the withheld replacement-cost depreciation?

C. No, the insured must still satisfy the policy's replacement-cost condition by proving the property was actually repaired or replaced — Dupree held an ACV appraisal award does not by itself entitle the insured to the depreciation/replacement-cost holdback; the insured must still comply with the policy's own replacement-cost condition, typically proof of completed repair or replacement.
Which case is the origin of the rule, later written into MCL 500.2833(1)(q), that a policy's suit-limitation clock tolls from notice of loss until formal denial of liability?

A. Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co (1976) — Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, 396 Mich 588 (1976), first held the limitation period tolls from notice until formal denial; the Legislature later codified this in MCL 500.2833(1)(q) by 1990 PA 305.

In Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, the insured's loss occurred December 14, 1971, notice was given around January 20, 1972, and the insurer formally denied liability June 22, 1972. Suit was filed March 16, 1973. Under the tolling rule, was the suit timely against a 12-month policy deadline?

A. Yes, because the clock was tolled for roughly 5 months during the notice-to-denial period, pushing the deadline to about mid-May 1973 — The Michigan Supreme Court tolled the 12-month clock for the approximately 5 months between notice (January 1972) and formal denial (June 1972), moving the effective deadline to roughly mid-May 1973, after the March 1973 filing.

What agency guidance, quoted in Cantina, stated that once an insurer determines a loss is covered, disagreements over whether claimed damages are part of the amount of loss are part of the appraisal process rather than a coverage question for the courts?

C. OFIS Bulletin 2006-07-INS and the December 2017 clarifying memorandum — OFIS Bulletin 2006-07-INS (later rescinded, then clarified by a December 2017 memorandum) stated that once coverage is admitted, amount-of-loss disagreements belong to the appraisal process, not the courts; these are agency guidance, not statutes.

A homeowner demands appraisal only 10 days after receiving the carrier's first estimate, before submitting a signed proof of loss or attempting any line-item reconciliation. What does MCL 500.2833(1)(m) itself say about a minimum waiting period before a demand is proper?

D. It sets no minimum waiting period; the trigger is simply a failure to agree on ACV or amount of loss — The statute's trigger is simply that the parties 'fail to agree' on ACV or amount of loss; it sets no minimum number of days that must first elapse, though an undocumented 'failure to agree' can invite a practical dispute over whether the demand is premature.
MCL 500.2833(1)(p) requires a covered loss to be paid within how many days after receipt of proof of amount of loss, subject to the withholding rule in MCL 500.2845?
D. 30 days — MCL 500.2833(1)(p) requires payment within 30 days after receipt of proof of amount of loss, except as otherwise provided in MCL 500.2845.
When was MCL 500.2833, the section containing today's appraisal clause and suit-limitation tolling rule, added to the Michigan Insurance Code, relative to the 1976 Tom Thomas decision?

D. 14 years after Tom Thomas, by 1990 PA 305 — MCL 500.2833 was added by 1990 PA 305, fourteen years after the Michigan Supreme Court's 1976 Tom Thomas decision that first announced the judge-made tolling doctrine the statute later codified.

A carrier's letter to an insured says only, 'we need additional documentation before we can determine coverage for these items; coverage for these items may be jeopardized if you do not respond.' Under Smitham as applied in Maksym, has this letter formally denied liability for those items?

D. No, because it is not explicit and does not unequivocally impress on the insured the need to pursue relief in court — Smitham v State Farm Fire & Cas Co (2012), applied in Maksym, requires a formal denial to be explicit and unequivocal; a request for more documentation with a warning that coverage 'may be jeopardized' does not meet that standard.
A restoration contractor with a 20 percent fee tied to the insurance recovery wants to name itself as the 'independent' party appraiser on its own job. Does White v State Farm authorize this?

C. No; White addressed a licensed appraiser's own compensation with disclosure, not a contractor with an unrelated financial stake naming itself appraiser on its own job — White v State Farm permits a party appraiser's own contingency-fee compensation with disclosure to the opposing party; it does not authorize a contractor with a separate financial interest in the outcome to appoint itself as appraiser, which raises independence and unlicensed-adjusting concerns instead.

A Michigan fire policy states that the suit clock is tolled 'in the event we formally deny liability.' The carrier pays part of the claim, never issues a denial, and then argues the one-year clock ran out. Under Smitham v State Farm Fire & Cas Co (2012), what happens to that policy language?

C. It is absolutely void under MCL 500.2860, because MCL 500.2833(1)(q) tolls without any such condition — Smitham held that policy language conditioning tolling on a formal denial is incompatible with MCL 500.2833(1)(q), which contains no such condition, and is therefore absolutely void under MCL 500.2860; Rory does not save policy language that conflicts with a statute.
